title: Why the Killer Mould Came From Downstairs
topic: Why Sir Alexander Fleming left his petri dishes uncovered (London, 1928)

lines: Sir Alexander Fleming left his petri dishes sitting out on a laboratory bench.
Bacteria were growing in Fleming's dishes.
When Alexander Fleming returned, one dish had a patch of mould.
Bacteria around the mould died. Bacteria farther away stayed normal.
Fleming said it was funny, then tested it again.
Fleming found the mould was Penicillium.
Fleming named the mould's weapon penicillin in 1929.
But at a microbiology congress in London, nobody believed Fleming.
Penicillin was too hard to isolate. It stayed mostly forgotten.
By 1936, the world still saw no value in penicillin.
You see, it is like one patch of mould on bread that stops everything around it from growing.
Here is the real reason. Penicillium mould travels through the air as spores.
In 1966, scientists traced Fleming's mould to La Touche's room, directly below his.
So the spores drifted up from downstairs and landed on the dishes Fleming left out.
The killer came from downstairs, not from Fleming's own bench.
That accident gave the world its first antibiotic.

claims.claim: Fleming left his culture plates on a bench in a corner of his laboratory; on his return he found one culture contaminated with a fungus, with the staphylococci colonies around the fungus destroyed and colonies farther away normal.
Fleming identified the mould as Penicillium and coined the name penicillin in 1929 for the antibacterial substance from the mould.
When Fleming spoke about the medical importance of penicillin at the Second International Congress of Microbiology held in London, no one believed him.
Penicillin was so difficult to isolate that its development as a drug seemed impossible, and Fleming did not convince anyone that his discovery was important.
Penicillin languished largely forgotten in the 1930s, and as late as 1936 there was no appreciation for penicillin.
The source of the fungal contaminant was established in 1966 as coming from La Touche's room, which was directly below Fleming's laboratory.
Penicillium chrysogenum is a ubiquitous airborne fungus detected in every sampled region of the Earth.
Penicillin was the first antibiotic substance discovered, and Fleming shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery of penicillin and its curative effect.
